catalog_quote: 3.2.17 Tonology. The language is tonal and it uses both lexical and grammatical tones to convey a message. These tones further changes in various phrases and clauses in relation to the context. 3.2.18 Lexical Tones. Six distinctive tones are heard in the language: The high, mid, low, falling, rising and high-mid. Thus, there are three level tones and three contour tones stated in table 20 below ... [p.466:] Within the scope of this research, no special chapter has been dedicatedto the study of tones. However, some evidence has been provided backing Mbuk as a tonal language. Some lexemes and clauses with similar segmental units have been differentiated in meaning with the change of tone. Hence, tone has been found to play a key semantic role at the lexical and grammatical level. The partial tone study has come up with seven tone systems: four levels and three contour tones.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mbuk is described as a tone language (lexical and grammatical tone; 3 level + 3 contour tones on p.165, revised to 4 level + 3 contour in the conclusion). The grammar's phonology chapter contains no statement on word stress or accent placement; stress is not treated as a category of Mbuk phonology.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only uses of 'stress' are non-technical (emphatic repetition favouring [ɪ] over [ə], p.163; impressionistic 'strength' on the F4 future marker, p.315).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone described at lexical and grammatical (clause) level; no word-prosodic prominence domain discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes Mbuk proper (Mbuk village, Bum subdivision, Boyo Division, NW Cameroon; ISO bpc, mbuk1244), explicitly distinguished from Chung/Cung (cung1238), with which SIL literature had lumped it as 'Chung-Bemboko'. Glottolog dates the thesis 2018 (title page 'March 2018'); the open PDF is the defended version dated 2022-01-10 and KPAAM-CAM lists it as 2021.

sources.note: Ch. 3 (pp.151-210) covers vowels, consonants, tonology (3.2.17-3.2.19, pp.165-167: 'The language is tonal..' six/seven tones), syllable and word structure, phonological processes; there is no section on stress or accent and word stress is never located. 'Stress' occurs only as emphasis conditioning a [ə~ɪ] variant (p.163) and an impressionistic remark that the F4 future marker may be pronounced with more 'strength.. such that one may think that it is stress' (p.315).
